title: Nosebleed After Drinking: Why It Happens and How to Stop It
excerpt: Why alcohol can give you a nosebleed, why it often starts the morning after, how ibuprofen, blood thinners and dry air play in, how to stop it, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why alcohol can trigger a nosebleed, the role of dry air and ibuprofen, how to stop it fast, and the warning signs that mean you should see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** an occasional nosebleed after a night of drinking is usually not dangerous. Alcohol widens the small blood vessels in your nose, makes your blood a little slower to clot, and dries you out. Add a dry bar or a heated bedroom, a stuffy nose you keep blowing, or a couple of ibuprofen before bed, and the fragile vessels just inside your nostrils can give way. Most of these bleeds stop within 10 to 15 minutes with simple pressure. What matters more is noticing when a nosebleed is a sign of something else: a fall you don't fully remember, a blood thinner mixed with alcohol, very high blood pressure, or bleeds that keep coming back.

**The quick rules:** Sit up, lean forward (not back), and pinch the soft part of your nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes without letting go to check. Breathe through your mouth and spit out any blood rather than swallowing it. Skip the painkillers that thin your blood, drink some water, and don't blow your nose hard for the rest of the day. If the bleeding won't stop after 20 minutes of steady pressure, is pouring heavily, or followed a hit to the head, get medical help.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article explains general causes and first aid. It is not medical advice. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** the bleeding is heavy and hasn't slowed after 20 minutes of firm pressure, you feel faint, dizzy, or short of breath, the nosebleed followed a fall, fight, or hit to the head or face, you are vomiting or coughing up blood, or you take a blood thinner such as warfarin, apixaban, or rivaroxaban and can't stop the bleeding. **Book a regular appointment if** you get nosebleeds after drinking more than once or twice, they come with easy bruising or bleeding gums, you have high blood pressure, or you drink heavily most days. Someone who has been drinking heavily every day and suddenly stops should also know that shakes, sweating, a racing heart, seeing or hearing things, or a seizure are withdrawal signs that need medical care, not something to wait out.

## Why Does Alcohol Give You a Nosebleed?

There isn't one single cause. Usually it's two or three small things stacking up on a set of blood vessels that were already easy to break.

### Your nose has a weak spot

Most nosebleeds start at the front of the nose, on the dividing wall between your nostrils (the septum). Doctors call this patch Kiesselbach's area, or Little's area. Several small arteries meet there in a tight web, sitting just under a thin, moist lining. Because it's right at the front, it gets the full blast of dry air every time you breathe in, and it's the part your fingers and tissues reach. That's why a nosebleed can start from something as small as a sneeze or a hard blow.

The back of the nose can bleed too (a posterior nosebleed), but that is much less common, tends to be heavier, and happens more often in older adults and people with high blood pressure or clotting problems. Those are the bleeds that more often need a doctor.

### Alcohol widens the blood vessels

Alcohol is a vasodilator, which means it relaxes and widens blood vessels near the surface of the body. That's the same effect behind the warm feeling and flushed cheeks after a drink or two. Inside your nose, those widened vessels swell and fill with more blood. The lining gets puffy (which is also why many people get a [stuffy nose after drinking](/never-hungover/stuffy-nose-after-drinking)), and the small vessels near the surface become easier to rupture.

Some people also release more histamine after drinking, especially with wine and beer. Histamine adds to the swelling and congestion. If your face goes red and blotchy when you drink, our guide to [red face after drinking](/never-hungover/red-face-after-drinking) explains what's happening there.

### Alcohol makes your blood a little slower to clot

Platelets are the tiny blood cells that plug a leak in the first few minutes after a vessel breaks. Alcohol can make platelets less sticky for a while after you drink, and heavy drinking can lower the number of platelets you have. The effect from one night out is modest, but it means a small bleed may take longer to seal than it would on a sober morning.

This isn't just theory. Researchers in the UK reported in the *BMJ* in the 1990s that adults admitted to hospital with nosebleeds were more likely to be regular drinkers than a comparison group, and that drinkers in the study had longer bleeding times. That kind of study can't prove alcohol caused the nosebleeds, but it fits with what we know about how alcohol affects clotting.

### Dehydration and dry air dry out the lining

Alcohol makes you pee more by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. After several drinks you are often a bit dehydrated, and that includes the moist lining inside your nose. Our explainer on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) covers how much fluid you actually lose and what helps.

Now add the setting. Bars and clubs are often air-conditioned or heated hard. Planes, ski trips, desert cities, and winter bedrooms with the heating on all have very dry air. You might sleep with your mouth open after drinking, then wake up with a dry, crusty nose. A dry lining cracks easily, and cracked lining over a web of swollen vessels is the classic setup for a nosebleed in the morning.

### Blowing, picking, and sneezing

When your nose is congested after drinking, you blow it more and harder. Crusts form overnight and people pick or rub at them half asleep. Sneezing fits are common in people who react to histamine or sulfites in wine. Every one of those is a small physical hit to an already fragile spot.

## Nosebleed the Morning After Drinking (With a Hangover)

A lot of people don't bleed while they're drinking. They wake up with a hangover and find blood on the pillow, or the bleed starts the first time they blow their nose. That timing makes sense:

- **You slept dehydrated in dry air**, often breathing through your mouth, so the lining dried and cracked overnight.
- **Crusts formed**, and blowing or wiping them off reopens the small tear.
- **You may have taken a painkiller** before bed or first thing in the morning, which can make bleeding harder to stop (more on that below).
- **You may have bumped your face** without remembering it, especially after a heavy night.

If the bleed is light, stops with pressure, and you feel otherwise normal apart from the hangover, it's very likely just the dry, irritated lining. Drink water, eat something, and leave your nose alone for the day. If you have a cut, swelling, or a bruise on your face, or a headache that feels different from your usual hangover headache, think carefully about whether you hit your head. A head injury plus alcohol is worth getting checked even if you feel okay, because drinking can mask the warning signs.

## Ibuprofen, Aspirin, and Other NSAIDs: A Common Hidden Trigger

This is the cause people most often miss. Many of us take an anti-inflammatory painkiller before bed after drinking, or as soon as we wake up with a headache. These drugs are called NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) and include ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), and aspirin.

- **Aspirin** blocks platelets from clumping for the whole life of each platelet, which is several days. That's why low-dose aspirin is used to prevent heart attacks. Even one dose can make a nosebleed last longer.
- **Ibuprofen and naproxen** also reduce platelet clumping, but the effect wears off as the drug leaves your body, usually within a day.
- **Alcohol on top** of either one adds its own small effect on clotting and on the stomach lining.

The combination doesn't usually cause a nosebleed by itself, but it can turn a tiny bleed that would have stopped in two minutes into one that drips for twenty. NSAID labels in the US already warn that people who have 3 or more drinks a day face a higher risk of stomach bleeding, which tells you the two don't sit well together.

If you get nosebleeds after drinking and you also tend to take a painkiller the same night or next morning, try dropping the painkiller and see whether the bleeds stop. Our guides on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) go into the timing and safer choices in detail.

Some supplements also affect clotting a little, including high-dose fish oil, vitamin E, ginkgo, and garlic pills. They're unlikely to matter on their own, but they can add up with alcohol and an NSAID. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take if your nosebleeds are frequent.

## Blood Thinners and Alcohol: When a Nosebleed Is More Serious

If you take a prescription blood thinner, a nosebleed after drinking deserves more respect. This group includes warfarin (Coumadin), the newer anticoagulants such as apixaban (Eliquis), rivaroxaban (Xarelto), and dabigatran (Pradaxa), and antiplatelet drugs such as clopidogrel (Plavix).

- **Warfarin and alcohol** have a well-known interaction. A bout of heavy drinking can make warfarin's effect stronger in the short term and raise your INR (the blood test that measures how thin your blood is), which raises bleeding risk. Long-term heavy drinking can have the opposite effect and make warfarin harder to control.
- **Other blood thinners** don't interact with alcohol in quite the same way, but alcohol still adds to bleeding risk and makes falls and injuries more likely.

On any of these medicines, a nosebleed that hasn't stopped after 15 to 20 minutes of firm pressure is a reason to get seen the same day, and heavy bleeding is a reason to go to the emergency room. Don't stop or skip a dose of your blood thinner on your own because of a nosebleed. Call the doctor who prescribed it. Our guide to [blood thinners and alcohol](/never-hungover/blood-thinners-and-alcohol) covers how much drinking is generally considered reasonable on each type, and when to talk to your doctor.

## Does Alcohol Raise Blood Pressure Enough to Cause a Nosebleed?

People often assume nosebleeds come from high blood pressure. The real link is less direct than most think.

Over one evening, a moderate amount of alcohol tends to lower blood pressure a little for a few hours, then it can rebound higher as the alcohol wears off. Regular heavy drinking is a well-established cause of long-term high blood pressure, and blood pressure usually improves when heavy drinkers cut back.

The research on blood pressure and nosebleeds is mixed. Studies have found that people with long-standing high blood pressure tend to have more severe nosebleeds and are more likely to need hospital treatment for them, probably because years of high pressure stiffen the vessels. But a nosebleed on its own is not a reliable sign that your blood pressure is high, and many people with very high readings never get one.

What this means in practice:

- If you've been told you have high blood pressure, nosebleeds after drinking are one more reason to get it checked and keep your drinking moderate.
- If a nosebleed comes with a severe headache, chest pain, blurred vision, confusion, or shortness of breath, treat that as an emergency. Those can be signs of a dangerously high blood pressure spike.
- If you've never had your blood pressure measured, a pharmacy machine or a quick visit to your doctor is an easy way to rule it out.

For more on how drinking affects blood pressure, see our guide on [alcohol and high blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025).

## Nosebleed After Drinking Wine (or Beer)

Some people only seem to bleed after red wine or certain beers. A few reasons this could happen:

- **Histamine.** Red wine and some beers contain more histamine than clear spirits. Histamine widens blood vessels and causes swelling and sneezing in people who are sensitive to it.
- **Sulfites.** Wine contains sulfites, which can trigger congestion and sneezing in some people, especially those with asthma.
- **Congestion from the drink itself.** Many people get a runny or blocked nose from wine and beer specifically, which means more blowing and more irritation.

If you notice the pattern, try switching to a clear spirit with a mixer, drinking water between drinks, and keeping your nose moist. If wine also gives you hives, wheezing, or a racing heart, that points more toward a sensitivity than an ordinary nosebleed, and it's worth mentioning to a doctor.

A less common cause worth knowing about: a genetic condition called hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) causes fragile, abnormal blood vessels, and frequent nosebleeds are its most common sign. Many people with HHT say alcohol, especially red wine, sets off their nosebleeds. If you have frequent nosebleeds that started young, small red spots on your lips, tongue, or fingertips, or close family members with the same problem, ask your doctor about it.

## Other Things That Can Happen on a Night Out

A few other causes are worth naming plainly, because they're common and people sometimes don't connect them.

- **Falls and knocks to the face.** Alcohol affects balance and reaction time. A bump against a door frame or a fall you barely remember can cause a nosebleed. If your nose looks crooked, is very swollen, or you can't breathe through one side, it may be broken. Get it checked within a few days.
- **Cocaine and other snorted drugs.** Snorting cocaine is one of the most common causes of nosebleeds in younger adults. It narrows blood vessels and damages the lining of the nose, and repeated use can wear a hole in the septum. Mixing it with alcohol also strains the heart. If this applies to you, it's worth being honest with a doctor, who has seen it many times and is there to help, not to judge.
- **Nasal sprays.** Steroid nasal sprays for allergies can dry and irritate the lining, especially if you aim them at the septum. Decongestant sprays used for more than a few days can cause rebound congestion and irritation.
- **Colds and allergies.** If you were already congested, drinking makes the swelling worse and the bleed more likely.

## Heavy Daily Drinking and Nosebleeds

For most social drinkers, the causes above explain the occasional nosebleed. It's a bit different for someone who has been drinking heavily most days for a long time.

Long-term heavy drinking can damage the liver, and the liver makes most of the proteins your blood needs to clot. It can also lower your platelet count. Together, these can lead to frequent or hard-to-stop nosebleeds, easy bruising, and bleeding gums. Signs that the liver may be involved include yellowing of the skin or eyes, a swollen belly, dark urine, or unusual tiredness.

If that sounds like you, the useful step is a simple blood test. A doctor can check your platelet count, clotting time, and liver function in one visit, and the results give you a clear picture instead of guessing. And if you drink heavily every day, don't stop suddenly without medical advice. Withdrawal can be dangerous, and a doctor can help you cut back safely.

## How to Stop a Nosebleed After Drinking: Step by Step

The good news is that almost every front-of-the-nose bleed stops with the right technique. Most people do it wrong by tipping their head back or checking too soon.

1. **Sit up and lean slightly forward.** This keeps blood from running down the back of your throat, where you'd swallow it. Swallowed blood (especially on a stomach already upset by alcohol) often makes people vomit.
2. **Pinch the soft part of your nose.** Use your thumb and index finger to squeeze both nostrils shut, just below the hard, bony bridge. Pinching the bone does nothing. The pressure needs to be on the soft part, where the bleeding vessels are.
3. **Hold it for 10 to 15 minutes by the clock.** Don't let go to peek. Releasing early breaks the clot that's starting to form, and you start over.
4. **Breathe through your mouth** and spit out any blood that reaches your throat.
5. **Cool things down if you like.** A cold pack or a bag of frozen peas on the bridge of your nose or the back of your neck is comfortable and may help a little, but pressure is what does the work.
6. **If it's still bleeding after 15 minutes,** pinch again for another 10 to 15 minutes. Some people find that one or two sprays of an over-the-counter decongestant nasal spray (oxymetazoline, sold as Afrin and similar) into the bleeding nostril before pinching helps narrow the vessels. Check the label first, and skip it if you have high blood pressure or a heart condition unless your doctor has said it's fine.
7. **If it's still going after about 20 minutes of steady pressure in total**, or it's heavy from the start, get medical help.

### What not to do

- **Don't tilt your head back.** It doesn't stop the bleed. It just sends blood down your throat.
- **Don't lie flat.** Same problem.
- **Don't stuff tissue deep into your nose.** Pulling it out later can tear the clot. Holding a tissue under your nose to catch drips is fine.
- **Don't have another drink to calm down.** More alcohol widens the vessels and slows clotting again.
- **Don't reach for aspirin or ibuprofen** for the headache while you're still bleeding.

## Aftercare: Stopping It From Starting Again

The clot that forms is fragile for the first day or two. A lot of people get a second bleed a few hours later because they blow their nose or bend over.

- **Don't blow your nose or pick at it for 24 hours.** If you have to sneeze, do it with your mouth open.
- **Avoid heavy lifting, hard exercise, and bending down** for the rest of the day.
- **Skip very hot drinks, hot showers, and more alcohol** for a day, since heat and alcohol both widen the vessels.
- **Keep the inside of your nose moist.** A saline nasal spray or gel a few times a day, or a thin smear of petroleum jelly just inside the nostril with a cotton swab, helps the lining heal.
- **Run a humidifier** in your bedroom if the air is dry, especially in winter or after a flight.
- **Drink water.** Rehydrating helps the lining recover, and it helps the rest of your hangover too.

## How to Make Nosebleeds After Drinking Less Likely

If this happens to you regularly, these are the changes most likely to help. None of them are complicated.

- **Drink less in one sitting.** The effects on blood vessels and clotting scale with how much you drink. Pacing to roughly one drink an hour and stopping earlier is the biggest lever.
- **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks helps with dehydration, and it naturally slows you down.
- **Put saline in your nose before bed** on nights you drink, especially in dry places. It takes ten seconds.
- **Use a bedroom humidifier** in winter or in dry climates.
- **Don't take aspirin or ibuprofen "just in case"** before bed after drinking. If you wake up with a headache, eat and drink water first, then decide.
- **Treat your allergies** so your nose isn't already irritated when you start drinking.
- **Notice your triggers.** If red wine is always the problem, switch drinks and see if the pattern stops.
- **Get your blood pressure checked** if you haven't in a while.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the drinking habits with the best evidence behind them, many of which also help here.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

To be clear up front: **there is no good evidence that DHM or any hangover supplement prevents or treats nosebleeds.** A nosebleed is a local problem with your nasal blood vessels, and pressure, moisture, and drinking less are what help.

That said, many people who search for this are also dealing with the rest of the morning after. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is in animals and lab settings, with only limited human data, so think of it as promising rather than proven. It isn't a reason to drink more, and it doesn't change any of the bleeding risks above. If you take a blood thinner or other regular medication, check with your pharmacist before adding any supplement.

If you'd like to try it for the general hangover side of things, two widely used options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands honestly.

## The Bottom Line

- An occasional nosebleed after drinking is common and usually harmless. Alcohol widens the vessels in your nose, slows clotting a little, and dries you out.
- Dry air, a stuffy nose you keep blowing, and an NSAID painkiller the same night are the most common extra triggers.
- To stop it, sit up, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose for 10 to 15 minutes without letting go. Don't tilt your head back.
- Get help if it won't stop after about 20 minutes, it's heavy, it followed a head injury, you feel faint, or you take a blood thinner.
- If nosebleeds keep happening, see a doctor. A blood pressure check and a simple blood test can rule out the less common causes.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get a nosebleed after drinking alcohol?**

Alcohol widens the small blood vessels in your nose, makes platelets a little less sticky so blood is slower to clot, and dehydrates you. The front of your nose already has a cluster of fragile vessels under a thin lining. Add dry air, congestion that makes you blow your nose hard, or an ibuprofen or aspirin, and one of those vessels can break. For most people an occasional bleed like this is not a sign of anything serious.

**Is a nosebleed after drinking dangerous?**

Usually not. Most nosebleeds after drinking come from the front of the nose and stop within 10 to 15 minutes of firm pressure. It becomes more serious if the bleeding is heavy or won't stop after about 20 minutes, it followed a fall or a hit to the head, you feel faint or short of breath, you're vomiting blood, or you take a blood thinner. In any of those cases, get medical help. Frequent nosebleeds are also worth a doctor's visit.

**Why do I get a nosebleed the morning after drinking?**

Sleeping after drinking often means sleeping dehydrated, sometimes with your mouth open, in dry indoor air. The lining of your nose dries and cracks overnight, crusts form, and the first time you blow or wipe your nose in the morning the small tear reopens. A painkiller taken before bed can make it bleed longer. If you have any bruising or swelling on your face, consider whether you might have hit your head.

**Can taking ibuprofen or aspirin after drinking cause a nosebleed?**

These painkillers don't usually cause a nosebleed by themselves, but they make it harder for your blood to clot, so a small bleed lasts longer. Aspirin's effect lasts for several days, while ibuprofen and naproxen wear off within about a day. Alcohol adds a small clotting effect of its own. If you get nosebleeds after drinking and also take a painkiller the same night, try skipping the painkiller and see if the pattern changes.

**Does alcohol raise blood pressure and cause nosebleeds?**

Regular heavy drinking is a well-known cause of long-term high blood pressure, and people with long-standing high blood pressure tend to have more severe nosebleeds. But a nosebleed on its own is not a reliable sign that your blood pressure is high, and a single night of moderate drinking usually doesn't spike it. If you get repeated nosebleeds, getting your blood pressure checked is a simple, sensible step. A nosebleed with a severe headache, chest pain, or blurred vision needs emergency care.

**How do you stop a nosebleed after drinking?**

Sit up and lean slightly forward, pinch the soft part of your nose just below the bony bridge, and hold firm pressure for 10 to 15 minutes without letting go to check. Breathe through your mouth and spit out blood instead of swallowing it. Don't tilt your head back or lie down. If it's still bleeding after about 20 minutes of steady pressure, or it's very heavy, get medical help.

**Can I drink alcohol if I take blood thinners and get nosebleeds?**

Talk to the doctor who prescribed your blood thinner. Alcohol adds to bleeding risk on any blood thinner, and heavy drinking can make warfarin's effect stronger and less predictable. If you get a nosebleed on a blood thinner that doesn't stop after 15 to 20 minutes of pressure, get seen the same day, and go to the emergency room if it's heavy. Don't skip doses on your own.

**Why do I only get nosebleeds after red wine?**

Red wine contains more histamine than most other drinks, along with sulfites. In sensitive people, these can cause swelling, congestion, and sneezing in the nose, which leads to more blowing and irritation. Switching to a clear spirit, drinking water between drinks, and keeping your nose moist often helps. If wine also gives you hives, wheezing, or a racing heart, mention it to a doctor.

**Can DHM prevent nosebleeds from drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM or any hangover supplement prevents nosebleeds. A nosebleed is a local problem with the blood vessels in your nose. Drinking less in one sitting, staying hydrated, keeping your nose moist, and avoiding blood-thinning painkillers are what help. DHM is studied for alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly in animals, and if you take a blood thinner you should check with a pharmacist before using any supplement.
